question: The term oscillation most nearly refers to a motion in which a body
opt_a: moves once from one place to another and then stops
opt_b: moves only in a circular path with constant speed
opt_c: keeps increasing its distance from a fixed point
opt_d: repeats about an equilibrium or mean position
explanation: Oscillation means repeated motion about an equilibrium or mean position. A swing, a simple pendulum, and a mass attached to a spring can all move to and fro about a central position. The body need not move along a straight line in every example, but there must be repeated departure from and return toward the mean position. Motion that simply continues in one direction is not oscillation, even if it is smooth. The central idea is repeated motion with a tendency to come back toward a reference position.

question: A motion repeats its state after equal intervals of time, but it does not move to and fro about a mean position. This motion is best described as
explanation: A periodic motion repeats itself after equal intervals of time. Oscillatory motion is more specific because it must be to-and-fro motion about an equilibrium or mean position. Uniform circular motion is a common example of periodic motion that is not normally called oscillatory motion of the body itself. Every oscillatory motion is periodic only when it repeats regularly, but every periodic motion is not necessarily oscillatory. The phrase “to and fro about a mean position” is the extra condition needed for oscillation.

question: In a playground swing, the lowest position of the seat is usually treated as the mean position. When the swing is pulled aside and released, why does it come back toward this position?
opt_a: The amplitude becomes zero at the extreme position
opt_b: A restoring tendency acts toward the mean position
opt_c: The time period changes direction at the mean position
opt_d: The frequency becomes larger near the extreme position
explanation: A swing displaced from its lowest position tends to return toward that position. This return is due to a restoring tendency that acts toward the mean or equilibrium position. The swing does not stop permanently at the mean position because it has inertia and can overshoot to the other side. Amplitude tells how far the swing goes from the mean position, not why it returns. The restoring tendency and inertia together produce the repeated motion.

question: A vibrating tuning fork is included among examples of oscillatory motion mainly because its prongs
opt_a: move to and fro about their normal positions
opt_b: move in one direction with increasing speed
opt_c: rotate steadily about the handle of the fork
opt_d: remain permanently bent after being struck
explanation: The prongs of a tuning fork vibrate about their normal positions after the fork is struck. This is an oscillatory motion because the prongs repeatedly move on opposite sides of an equilibrium position. The motion is called vibratory because the oscillations are rapid. Steady rotation or one-way motion would not describe the back-and-forth nature of the prong motion. The normal position is important because displacement is measured from that reference position.

question: For an oscillator, the symbol \(x\) most commonly represents
opt_a: the total distance covered in many oscillations
opt_b: the time taken for one complete oscillation
opt_c: the mass of the oscillating body
explanation: In oscillations, \(x\) usually denotes the displacement of the body from its mean position at a particular instant. It can be positive on one side of the mean position and negative on the other side, depending on the chosen sign convention. The total distance travelled is different from \(x\), because distance keeps adding while displacement depends on position relative to the mean point. Mass is usually denoted by \(m\), and the time period is denoted by \(T\). The sign of \(x\) helps describe which side of the mean position the body is on.

question:
Study the table and identify the row in which the symbol and unit are not properly paired.
RowQuantityUsual symbolSI unit
PDisplacement from mean position\(x\)\(\text{m}\)
QAmplitude\(A\)\(\text{m}\)
RTime period\(T\)\(\text{s}\)
SFrequency\(f\)\(\text{rad s}^{-1}\)
explanation: Displacement \(x\) and amplitude \(A\) are lengths, so their SI unit is \(\text{m}\). Time period \(T\) is the time for one complete oscillation, so its unit is \(\text{s}\). Frequency \(f\) means the number of oscillations per unit time, and its SI unit is \(\text{Hz}\) or \(\text{s}^{-1}\). The unit \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\) is used for angular frequency \(\omega\), not ordinary frequency \(f\). The factor \(2\pi\) separates \(\omega\) from \(f\), so their units should not be interchanged casually.

question: A block attached to a horizontal spring is pulled slightly and released on a smooth surface. The motion is described as oscillatory because the block
opt_a: has a large mass compared with the spring
opt_b: moves only when an external force keeps pushing it
opt_c: moves back and forth about its equilibrium position
opt_d: covers equal distances in every equal interval of time
explanation: A spring-block system can oscillate because the spring provides a restoring force when the block is displaced from equilibrium. After release, the block moves toward the equilibrium position and may continue to the other side due to inertia. This repeated back-and-forth motion is the key feature of oscillation. Equal distances in equal intervals would suggest uniform motion, not the usual motion of an oscillator. The equilibrium position is the reference point about which the displacement changes sign.

question: The amplitude \(A\) of an oscillator is
opt_a: maximum displacement from the mean position
opt_b: the total distance travelled in one complete oscillation
opt_c: the time required to go from one extreme to the other
opt_d: the number of oscillations completed per second
explanation: Amplitude \(A\) is the greatest distance of the oscillator from its mean position on either side. It is a length, so its SI unit is \(\text{m}\). The total distance travelled in one complete oscillation may be related to amplitude in special cases, but it is not the definition of amplitude. Time period and frequency describe timing, while amplitude describes the maximum displacement. Amplitude is measured from the mean position, not from one extreme position to the other.

question: During one complete oscillation, the time taken is called the
explanation: The time period \(T\) is the time taken by an oscillating body to complete one full oscillation. It is measured in seconds, written as \(\text{s}\). Frequency \(f\) counts how many oscillations occur in one second, so it is linked to \(T\) but is not the same quantity. Amplitude \(A\) gives the maximum displacement, not the duration of the motion. A complete oscillation means the body returns to the same state of motion, not merely to the same position once.

question: An oscillator completes \(12\) oscillations in \(3.0\,\text{s}\). Its frequency is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Number of oscillations \(N=12\), time taken \(t=3.0\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Frequency \(f\).
Frequency means number of complete oscillations per unit time.
The useful relation is
\[
f=\frac{N}{t}
\]
Substitute the given values:
\[
f=\frac{12}{3.0\,\text{s}}
\]
Calculate the quotient:
\[
f=4.0\,\text{s}^{-1}
\]
Since \(\text{s}^{-1}\) for oscillations is written as \(\text{Hz}\), the result is \(4.0\,\text{Hz}\).
The option \(36\,\text{Hz}\) comes from multiplying \(12\) and \(3.0\), but frequency requires division by the total time.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(f=4.0\,\text{Hz}\).

question: The unit \(\text{Hz}\) is used for the quantity that tells
explanation: The unit \(\text{Hz}\) is used for frequency \(f\). A frequency of \(1\,\text{Hz}\) means one complete oscillation per second. Maximum displacement is amplitude \(A\), and its SI unit is \(\text{m}\). The time taken for one oscillation is time period \(T\), and its unit is \(\text{s}\). Frequency and time period are reciprocal quantities, so their meanings should not be swapped.

question: For an oscillator with time period \(T=0.50\,\text{s}\), the frequency is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Time period \(T=0.50\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Required:} \) Frequency \(f\).
For periodic or oscillatory motion, frequency and time period are related by
\[
f=\frac{1}{T}
\]
This relation applies because \(T\) is the time for one oscillation, while \(f\) is the number of oscillations per second.
Substitute \(T=0.50\,\text{s}\):
\[
f=\frac{1}{0.50\,\text{s}}
\]
\[
f=2.0\,\text{s}^{-1}
\]
For oscillations, \(\text{s}^{-1}\) is written as \(\text{Hz}\).
The value \(0.50\,\text{Hz}\) would repeat the time period as if it were frequency, which reverses the reciprocal relation.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(f=2.0\,\text{Hz}\).

question: A note about an oscillator says: “The body is at the extreme position when \(|x|=A\).” This statement means that
opt_a: the body is at the mean position
opt_b: the body has completed exactly one oscillation
opt_d: the frequency has become equal to the amplitude
explanation: The symbol \(x\) represents instantaneous displacement from the mean position. The symbol \(A\) represents amplitude, which is the maximum magnitude of \(x\). Therefore, \(|x|=A\) means the body is at one of its extreme positions. The absolute value is used because the extreme can be on the \(+\) side or the \(-\) side of the mean position. Frequency is a time-related quantity, so it cannot become equal to a length like amplitude.

question: In an oscillating system, the restoring tendency is directed
opt_a: away from the mean position on both sides
opt_b: only when the body is exactly at an extreme position
opt_c: only along the positive side of the chosen axis
opt_d: toward the mean position when the body is displaced
explanation: A restoring tendency is the tendency that tries to bring the displaced body back toward its equilibrium or mean position. If the body is displaced to the positive side, the restoring effect is toward the negative direction, and if it is displaced to the negative side, it is toward the positive direction. This direction is why the motion can reverse again and again. The restoring tendency need not always have the same direction in space; it depends on which side of the mean position the body occupies. At the mean position, the displacement from equilibrium is zero, so the restoring effect is not described as pulling it farther away.

question:
Match the basic oscillation symbols with their usual meanings.
Column IColumn II
P. \(A\)1. Time for one complete oscillation
Q. \(T\)2. Number of oscillations per second
R. \(f\)3. Maximum displacement from mean position
S. \(\omega\)4. Angular frequency
explanation: Amplitude \(A\) is the maximum displacement from the mean position. Time period \(T\) is the time required for one complete oscillation. Frequency \(f\) is the number of complete oscillations per second. Angular frequency \(\omega\) is related to frequency by \(\omega=2\pi f\). The distinction between \(f\) and \(\omega\) matters because \(\omega\) measures angular phase change per unit time, while \(f\) counts cycles per unit time.

question:
Use the graph description below.
The displacement \(x\) of an oscillating body is plotted against time \(t\). The curve repeats smoothly above and below the mean line \(x=0\), and the highest positive value of \(x\) is \(+A\).
The value \(+A\) on this graph represents
opt_c: the angular frequency of the motion
explanation: On an \(x-t\) graph, the vertical coordinate gives displacement \(x\) from the mean position. The line \(x=0\) represents the mean position. The highest positive value \(+A\) is the extreme displacement on the positive side, so its magnitude is the amplitude. Time period would be read along the time axis as the interval after which the graph repeats. Frequency and angular frequency are obtained from timing information, not from the vertical height alone.

question: Use the arrangement described below. A pendulum bob moves along an arc through three marked positions: left extreme \(L\), lowest point \(M\), and right extreme \(R\). For small oscillations, the position usually treated as the mean position is
opt_a: \(L\), because the bob pauses there momentarily
opt_b: \(R\), because the bob pauses there momentarily
opt_c: \(M\), because it is the equilibrium position
opt_d: any point on the arc, because all positions repeat
explanation: In a simple pendulum, the lowest point \(M\) is the equilibrium or mean position for small oscillations. The bob moves to and fro about this point as it swings between the two extremes. At \(L\) and \(R\), the bob is farthest from the mean position, so those are extreme positions rather than the mean position. The bob may momentarily stop at an extreme, but stopping for an instant does not make that point the equilibrium position. The mean position is chosen from force balance and symmetry, not from where the bob’s speed happens to be zero.

question: The relation connecting angular frequency \(\omega\) and ordinary frequency \(f\) is best completed as \(\omega=\underline{\hspace{1.5cm}}\).
explanation:
\( \textbf{Known idea:} \) Ordinary frequency \(f\) counts complete cycles per second.
Angular frequency \(\omega\) measures angular phase change per second.
One complete cycle corresponds to an angular change of \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\).
So, angular change per second equals \(2\pi\) times the number of cycles per second.
The relation is
\[
\omega=2\pi f
\]
The unit of \(f\) is \(\text{Hz}\), or \(\text{s}^{-1}\).
The unit of \(\omega\) is commonly written as \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\).
Using \(\frac{f}{2\pi}\) would reduce the value instead of converting cycles per second into radians per second.
The factor \(2\pi\) appears because each complete oscillation corresponds to one full phase cycle.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\omega=2\pi f\).

question: A body passes through its mean position during an oscillation. At that instant, its displacement \(x\) from the mean position is
explanation: The displacement \(x\) in oscillatory motion is measured from the mean or equilibrium position. When the body is exactly at the mean position, its position coincides with the reference point from which \(x\) is measured. Therefore, the instantaneous displacement is \(0\), even though the body may be moving. The values \(+A\) and \(-A\) correspond to extreme positions on the two sides of the mean position. Displacement should not be confused with speed, because a body can have zero displacement from the mean position and still be in motion.

question: A motion has frequency \(5\,\text{Hz}\). The number of complete oscillations made in \(20\,\text{s}\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Frequency \(f=5\,\text{Hz}\) and time \(t=20\,\text{s}\).
Frequency \(5\,\text{Hz}\) means \(5\) complete oscillations occur in \(1\,\text{s}\).
The required number of oscillations is \(N\).
Use the relation
\[
N=ft
\]
Substitute the values:
\[
N=(5\,\text{s}^{-1})(20\,\text{s})
\]
The unit \(\text{s}^{-1}\) cancels with \(\text{s}\).
\[
N=100
\]
The answer is a pure number because it counts complete oscillations.
The option \(4\) would come from using \(\frac{20}{5}\), which gives time per oscillation only if the given \(5\) were a time period.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(100\) complete oscillations.

question: A clock hand returns to the same orientation after equal intervals of time, but it does not move to and fro about a central mean position. This is an example of
opt_a: periodic motion that is not oscillatory
opt_b: oscillatory motion that is not periodic
opt_c: simple harmonic motion with variable amplitude
explanation: The motion of a clock hand repeats after equal time intervals, so it is periodic. However, the hand does not move back and forth about a mean position; it rotates continuously in the same sense. Oscillatory motion needs motion on opposite sides of an equilibrium or mean position. Periodic motion is therefore a broader idea than oscillatory motion. The repeated configuration alone is not enough to call a motion oscillatory.

question:
The statement pair below refers to repeated motion.
I. A motion that repeats after equal intervals of time is periodic.
II. Every periodic motion must be to-and-fro motion about a mean position.
Select the valid evaluation.
opt_a: Both I and II are valid
opt_b: I is valid, but II is not valid
opt_c: I is not valid, but II is valid
opt_d: Neither I nor II is valid
explanation: Statement I gives the basic meaning of periodic motion: the motion repeats itself after equal intervals of time. Statement II adds a condition that belongs to oscillatory motion, not to every periodic motion. A body moving uniformly in a circle is periodic because it returns to the same position after each revolution. Still, it is not usually described as to-and-fro motion about a mean position. This distinction prevents the broader idea of periodicity from being narrowed incorrectly to only back-and-forth motion.

question: A signal repeats its entire pattern every \(0.02\,\text{s}\). Its time period and frequency are respectively
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given information:} \) The complete pattern repeats every \(0.02\,\text{s}\).
This repeating time is the time period:
\[
T=0.02\,\text{s}
\]
Frequency is the reciprocal of time period:
\[
f=\frac{1}{T}
\]
Substitute the value:
\[
f=\frac{1}{0.02\,\text{s}}
\]
Write \(0.02\) as \(2\times10^{-2}\):
\[
f=\frac{1}{2\times10^{-2}}\,\text{s}^{-1}
\]
\[
f=50\,\text{s}^{-1}
\]
For repeated cycles, \(\text{s}^{-1}\) is written as \(\text{Hz}\).
A small time period corresponds to a large frequency, so \(0.02\,\text{Hz}\) would reverse the reciprocal relation.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(T=0.02\,\text{s}\) and \(f=50\,\text{Hz}\).

question:
Study the table and choose the row that best separates periodic and oscillatory motion.
RowPeriodic motionOscillatory motion
PRepeats after equal intervals of timeMoves to and fro about a mean position
QAlways has amplitude \(A\)Never repeats with time
RRequires a spring onlyRequires circular motion only
SHas no fixed time intervalMoves only in one direction
explanation: Periodic motion is identified by repetition after equal intervals of time. Oscillatory motion is identified by to-and-fro motion about a mean or equilibrium position. Row P states these two meanings without forcing one to be identical to the other. Row Q is wrong because oscillatory motion may repeat regularly, and periodic motion does not always need an amplitude measured from a mean position. Rows R and S restrict the ideas to unsuitable special cases, while the definitions are much broader.

question: A body performs repeated motion, but each repetition takes a different amount of time. Based only on this information, the motion should not be classified as
opt_d: repeated motion in a broad sense
explanation: Strictly periodic motion requires repetition after equal intervals of time. If each repetition takes a different duration, the motion may still look repeated in a loose sense, but it does not satisfy the precise condition for periodic motion. Changing speed is not enough to reject periodicity, because many periodic motions have variable speed. The key issue here is unequal repeat times, not whether the motion is fast or slow. A truly periodic motion has a fixed time period \(T\).

question:
Assertion: Uniform circular motion is periodic.
Reason: In uniform circular motion, the body returns to the same position after every fixed time interval.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: Uniform circular motion is periodic because the body completes each revolution in the same time when its speed is constant. After every revolution, it returns to the same position with the same direction of motion. The Reason states exactly the condition needed for periodic motion: repetition after a fixed interval. This does not automatically make the motion oscillatory, because the body is not moving to and fro about a mean position. Periodicity here comes from repeated circular configuration, not from back-and-forth displacement along a line.

question: A rotating fan blade seen at a fixed mark crosses the mark at regular intervals. The crossing pattern is periodic because
opt_a: the blade changes its length during rotation
opt_b: the blade moves to and fro along a diameter
opt_c: the blade has zero acceleration throughout
explanation: A rotating fan blade can produce a repeated configuration at a fixed mark after equal intervals of time. This regular repetition is the defining feature of periodic motion. The blade does not need to move to and fro along a diameter for the motion to be periodic. It also does not have zero acceleration in circular motion, because its direction of velocity changes continuously. The repeated arrival at the same configuration is the time-based feature that matters here.

question:
A motion is represented by the following record.
At \(t=0\,\text{s}\), \(2\,\text{s}\), \(4\,\text{s}\), and \(6\,\text{s}\), the moving object is found in the same state of motion. Between these instants, its motion follows the same pattern again and again.
The time period of the motion is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Observation from the record:} \) The same state appears at \(t=0\,\text{s}\), \(2\,\text{s}\), \(4\,\text{s}\), and \(6\,\text{s}\).
The time interval between successive identical states is
\[
2\,\text{s}-0\,\text{s}=2\,\text{s}
\]
Also,
\[
4\,\text{s}-2\,\text{s}=2\,\text{s}
\]
and
\[
6\,\text{s}-4\,\text{s}=2\,\text{s}
\]
The repeated interval is therefore \(2\,\text{s}\).
The time period \(T\) is the least regular time after which the same state repeats.
Choosing \(4\,\text{s}\) would skip one repetition and give a multiple of the actual period.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(T=2\,\text{s}\).

question: An oscillatory motion is better described as motion in which the body
opt_a: moves away from the starting point without returning
opt_b: repeats only its speed but not its position
opt_c: moves in a circle with constant speed only
opt_d: moves to and fro about a mean position
explanation: Oscillatory motion involves repeated motion on the two sides of a mean or equilibrium position. A pendulum bob, a vibrating string, and a spring-block system are familiar examples. The phrase “to and fro” is important because it separates oscillation from motion that merely repeats in a circular path. Repetition of speed alone is not enough, because the position and direction pattern must also be considered. The mean position acts as the reference about which the displacement changes with time.

question: In a spring-block oscillator on a horizontal smooth surface, the block crosses the equilibrium position and continues to the other side mainly because
opt_a: its inertia carries it beyond the equilibrium position
opt_b: the spring force is maximum at the equilibrium position
opt_c: the amplitude becomes infinite at the equilibrium position
opt_d: the time period becomes zero at the equilibrium position
explanation: When the block reaches the equilibrium position, the restoring force of an ideal spring is zero at that instant. However, the block has velocity as it reaches that position. Due to inertia, it does not stop immediately and continues to the other side. Once it moves beyond equilibrium, the spring force acts back toward the equilibrium position. Oscillation results from the restoring force pulling toward equilibrium and inertia carrying the body through it.

question: Vibratory motion is commonly understood as
opt_a: very slow circular motion about a fixed centre
opt_c: motion that repeats without any displacement
opt_d: motion possible only for planets around the Sun
explanation: Vibratory motion is a type of oscillatory motion that occurs rapidly. The prongs of a tuning fork, a stretched string, and the surface of a drum can vibrate about their equilibrium positions. The motion is still back and forth, but the time period is usually small. It is not restricted to circular motion or astronomical motion. The word “vibration” emphasizes rapid repeated displacement about a normal position.

question:
The following examples are listed:
I. A pendulum bob swinging through small angles
II. A tuning fork prong moving after being struck
III. The second hand of a clock rotating uniformly
The examples that are oscillatory are
explanation: A pendulum bob swinging through small angles moves to and fro about its mean position, so it is oscillatory. A tuning fork prong also moves rapidly to and fro about its normal position, so it is vibratory and hence oscillatory. The second hand of a clock repeats its motion after equal times, but it rotates in one sense rather than moving to and fro about a mean position. This makes the clock hand periodic but not oscillatory in the usual sense. The deciding feature is back-and-forth motion about equilibrium, not repetition alone.

question: A stretched string is plucked at its middle and then released. The middle point of the string moves on both sides of its normal position. This motion is classified as oscillatory because
opt_a: the string gains mass during motion
opt_b: the motion is repeated about an equilibrium position
opt_c: the string moves only in one direction after release
opt_d: the amplitude is equal to the time period
explanation: When a stretched string is plucked, its particles are displaced from their normal positions. After release, the restoring effect due to tension pulls them back toward equilibrium. The particles can pass through their normal positions and move to the other side, producing repeated to-and-fro motion. This is why the motion is oscillatory or vibratory. Amplitude is a length and time period is a time, so treating them as equal quantities is not physically meaningful.

question: Use the arrangement described below. A bead can slide without friction along a straight horizontal rod. It is attached to two identical light springs, one on each side, fixed to rigid walls. When the bead is displaced slightly to the right and released, the most suitable description of its subsequent motion is
opt_a: one-way motion to the right only
opt_b: to-and-fro motion about the central point
opt_c: uniform circular motion about the midpoint
opt_d: random motion because two springs are attached
explanation: With identical springs on both sides, the central position is the equilibrium position of the bead. If the bead is moved to the right, one spring is compressed and the other is stretched in a way that produces a restoring effect toward the centre. After reaching the centre, the bead can continue to the left because it has inertia. The same restoring tendency then acts back toward the centre from the left side. The two-spring arrangement therefore supports oscillatory motion about the central equilibrium point.

question: A body moves along a straight line and repeatedly passes through a fixed point \(O\). Which additional condition is most necessary to call the motion oscillatory about \(O\)?
opt_a: \(O\) is a stable equilibrium position and the body moves on both sides of it
opt_b: the body has the same speed every time it crosses \(O\)
opt_c: the body covers the same total distance in every second
opt_d: the acceleration is always zero at \(O\)
explanation: Repeatedly crossing a point does not by itself prove oscillatory motion. For motion to be oscillatory about \(O\), the point \(O\) must act as a stable equilibrium or mean position. A small displacement from \(O\) should produce a restoring tendency toward \(O\). The body should also move on the two sides of \(O\), so the motion is genuinely to and fro about that point. Having the same crossing speed, covering equal distance per second, or having zero acceleration at \(O\) is not the defining condition. Therefore, the required extra condition is that \(O\) is a stable equilibrium position and the motion occurs on both sides of it.

question: In an oscillating system, stable equilibrium is important because a small displacement from it usually produces
opt_a: a tendency to move farther away from the equilibrium position
opt_b: no possible motion on either side of the equilibrium position
opt_c: a tendency to return toward the equilibrium position
opt_d: a constant velocity away from the equilibrium position
explanation: Stable equilibrium means that when the body is displaced slightly, the system tends to bring it back toward the equilibrium position. This returning tendency is essential for oscillatory motion. If a displacement made the body move farther away, the equilibrium would not support ordinary oscillations about that point. Inertia may carry the body past the equilibrium position, but the restoring tendency keeps redirecting the motion toward it. Stability gives the mean position its role as the centre of repeated motion.

question: A ball is kept at the bottom of a smooth bowl and then displaced slightly to one side. The bottom of the bowl represents a stable equilibrium position because the ball
opt_a: tends to move farther from the bottom
opt_b: moves only if the bowl supplies no force
opt_c: has zero restoring tendency after displacement
opt_d: tends to return toward the bottom
explanation: A stable equilibrium position is one from which a small displacement produces a tendency to return. The bottom of a smooth bowl is a good example because gravity has a component that pulls the ball back toward the lowest point when it is displaced. If the ball has speed, it may pass through the bottom and rise on the other side, giving repeated motion. An unstable position would instead make the body move farther away after a small displacement. The returning tendency is what allows the lowest point to act as the centre of oscillation.

question: In an oscillating system, the body overshoots the mean position after returning to it mainly due to
opt_b: disappearance of mass at the mean position
opt_c: increase of amplitude at every crossing
opt_d: permanent reversal of the restoring tendency
explanation: The restoring tendency brings the displaced body back toward the mean position. When the body reaches the mean position, it generally has speed, so it cannot stop instantly. Due to inertia, it continues beyond the mean position and reaches the other side. After crossing the mean position, the restoring tendency acts in the opposite direction, again toward the centre. Oscillation needs both a restoring tendency and the inertia that carries the body past equilibrium.

question:
Assertion: A stable equilibrium position can act as the mean position for oscillations.
Reason: Near stable equilibrium, a small displacement usually gives a restoring tendency toward the equilibrium position.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: A stable equilibrium position is suitable as the mean position of an oscillator because the system tends to return to it after a small displacement. That returning tendency is the physical reason repeated motion can occur about that position. The Reason correctly states the behavior near stable equilibrium. It also explains why an unstable equilibrium is not normally the centre of a steady oscillation. The mean position in oscillation is not chosen randomly; it is tied to the stability of the system.

question:
Study the table and identify the row that gives the most suitable restoring-tendency description.
RowDisplacement from mean positionRestoring tendency
PTo the rightToward the right
QTo the rightToward the left
RTo the leftToward the left
SOn either sideAway from the mean position
explanation: A restoring tendency always acts toward the mean position when the body is displaced. If the body is displaced to the right of the mean position, the restoring tendency must be toward the left. Row Q describes this direction relation. If the body were displaced to the left, the restoring tendency would be toward the right. The direction of the restoring effect changes with the side of displacement, so it cannot be fixed permanently to one side.

question: In a one-dimensional oscillator, the mean position is chosen as \(O\). If displacement to the right is taken positive, then a body \(3\,\text{cm}\) to the left of \(O\) has displacement
explanation: Displacement in one-dimensional oscillatory motion is measured from the mean position with a chosen sign convention. If the right side is positive, the left side must be negative. A position \(3\,\text{cm}\) to the left of the mean position is therefore written as \(-3\,\text{cm}\). The magnitude of the displacement is \(3\,\text{cm}\), but the signed displacement includes direction along the chosen axis. The sign tells the side of the mean position, not whether the motion is speeding up or slowing down.

question: A body moves from the left extreme to the right extreme through the mean position. If the amplitude is \(A\), the displacement changes from
explanation: Amplitude \(A\) is the maximum magnitude of displacement from the mean position. If the positive side is chosen toward the right, the right extreme has displacement \(+A\). The left extreme then has displacement \(-A\). Moving from left extreme to right extreme changes the signed displacement from \(-A\) through \(0\) to \(+A\). The total distance covered in that motion is \(2A\), but the displacement values at the two extremes are signed positions relative to the mean point.

question:
Read the record below and answer the question.
An oscillator moves along a straight line. Its mean position is \(M\). At one instant it is \(4\,\text{cm}\) to the right of \(M\), and later it is \(4\,\text{cm}\) to the left of \(M\). The positive direction is chosen to the right.
The two displacement values are respectively
explanation: The sign of displacement depends on the chosen positive direction. Since the right side is positive, a position \(4\,\text{cm}\) to the right of \(M\) is written as \(+4\,\text{cm}\). A position \(4\,\text{cm}\) to the left of \(M\) is written as \(-4\,\text{cm}\). The two positions have the same distance from the mean position but opposite signed displacements. This is why displacement in oscillation is not described by magnitude alone.

question: The displacement \(x\) of an oscillator is zero at a certain instant. This does not necessarily mean that
opt_a: the body is at the mean position
opt_b: the reference point for \(x\) is the mean position
opt_c: the body is at zero distance from the mean position
opt_d: the body is at rest at that instant
explanation: If \(x=0\), the body is at the mean position because displacement is measured from that point. However, being at the mean position does not mean the body must be at rest. In many oscillations, the body passes through the mean position with a considerable speed. Rest occurs momentarily at extreme positions in many ideal oscillators, not at every mean-position crossing. The value of displacement tells position relative to the mean point, not the complete state of motion.

question:
Use the graph description below.
A displacement-time graph of an oscillator crosses the horizontal axis at \(t=t_1\). The horizontal axis represents \(x=0\).
At \(t=t_1\), the graph shows that the oscillator is
explanation: In a displacement-time graph, the vertical coordinate gives \(x\), the displacement from the mean position. The horizontal axis represents \(x=0\). When the graph crosses this axis, the oscillator is passing through the mean position. This crossing alone does not tell whether the body is moving in the positive or negative direction; that depends on the slope of the graph at the crossing. The graph location gives position, while the graph slope gives information about velocity.

question: A body oscillates between two extreme positions separated by \(10\,\text{cm}\). Its amplitude is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given information:} \) Distance between the two extreme positions \(=10\,\text{cm}\).
The mean position lies midway between the two extremes for a symmetric oscillation.
Amplitude is the distance from the mean position to either extreme.
Therefore,
\[
A=\frac{\text{distance between extremes}}{2}
\]
Substitute the value:
\[
A=\frac{10\,\text{cm}}{2}
\]
\[
A=5\,\text{cm}
\]
The value \(10\,\text{cm}\) is the extreme-to-extreme separation, not the amplitude.
Amplitude is measured from the mean position to one extreme only.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(A=5\,\text{cm}\).

question: The amplitude of an oscillation is not the same as the total distance covered in one complete oscillation because amplitude measures
opt_a: the maximum displacement from the mean position only
opt_b: the number of oscillations per second only
opt_c: the complete path from one extreme to the other and back
opt_d: the angular phase change per second only
explanation: Amplitude \(A\) is a position measure: it gives the maximum distance of the body from the mean position. In a complete oscillation between two extremes, the body covers several parts of the path, so the distance travelled can be larger than \(A\). For the usual motion from one extreme to the other and back to the starting extreme, the total path length is \(4A\). Frequency and angular frequency describe timing, not the size of the oscillation. The phrase “maximum displacement” should be read as distance from the mean position, not total path length.

question:
The following statements refer to amplitude.
I. Amplitude has the same unit as displacement.
II. Larger amplitude means the extreme position is farther from the mean position.
III. Amplitude is always equal to the time period.
Select the valid set.
explanation: Amplitude is the maximum magnitude of displacement from the mean position, so it has the same unit as displacement. In SI, both amplitude and displacement are measured in \(\text{m}\). If the amplitude is larger, the extreme position is farther from the mean position. Statement III is not valid because amplitude is a length, while time period is a time. Quantities with different physical dimensions cannot be equal in the ordinary physical sense.

question: For a simple oscillator, \(x=+A\) and \(x=-A\) represent
opt_a: opposite extreme positions about the mean
opt_b: two different mean positions of the same oscillator
opt_d: two instants where displacement is zero
explanation: The symbols \(+A\) and \(-A\) are signed displacement values. They represent equal maximum distances from the mean position on opposite sides. The sign tells the side of the mean position according to the chosen axis. Both positions are extreme positions because the magnitude of displacement is \(A\). They do not represent different frequencies, because frequency is a timing property of the whole repeated motion.

question: A mass-spring system is pulled farther from its equilibrium position before release, while the spring remains in its ideal range. The immediate effect on amplitude is that it
opt_a: decreases because the spring becomes stiffer
opt_c: stays unchanged because the period is unchanged
opt_d: becomes equal to the extreme-to-extreme distance
explanation: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position. If the mass is pulled farther before release, the starting extreme displacement is larger. As long as the spring remains in its ideal working range and the release is from rest, that larger displacement becomes the amplitude of the oscillation. This does not mean amplitude is the same kind of quantity as frequency or time period. The size of the oscillation is being changed, not the meaning of the timing quantities.

question: An oscillator has frequency \(8\,\text{Hz}\). Its time period is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Frequency \(f=8\,\text{Hz}=8\,\text{s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Required:} \) Time period \(T\).
Frequency and time period are reciprocal:
\[
T=\frac{1}{f}
\]
Substitute \(f=8\,\text{s}^{-1}\):
\[
T=\frac{1}{8\,\text{s}^{-1}}
\]
\[
T=0.125\,\text{s}
\]
The unit becomes seconds because \(T\) measures time per oscillation.
The option \(8\,\text{s}\) treats frequency as though it were already a time period.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(T=0.125\,\text{s}\).

question: A displacement-time graph repeats after every \(0.40\,\text{s}\). The angular frequency of the motion is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) The graph repeats after \(0.40\,\text{s}\), so \(T=0.40\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Required:} \) Angular frequency \(\omega\).
The relation between angular frequency and time period is
\[
\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}
\]
This applies because one complete oscillation corresponds to a phase change of \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\).
Substitute \(T=0.40\,\text{s}\):
\[
\omega=\frac{2\pi}{0.40\,\text{s}}
\]
Since \(0.40=\frac{2}{5}\),
\[
\omega=2\pi\times\frac{5}{2}\,\text{s}^{-1}
\]
\[
\omega=5\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
The unit \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\) belongs to angular frequency, not to ordinary frequency.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\omega=5\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\).

question: A record of an oscillation gives \(f=3\,\text{Hz}\). The angular frequency \(\omega\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Ordinary frequency \(f=3\,\text{Hz}\).
Angular frequency \(\omega\) is the rate of phase change in radians per second.
One complete oscillation corresponds to a phase change of \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\).
Use the relation
\[
\omega=2\pi f
\]
Substitute \(f=3\,\text{s}^{-1}\):
\[
\omega=2\pi(3\,\text{s}^{-1})
\]
\[
\omega=6\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
The factor \(2\pi\) converts cycles per second into radians per second.
Dividing by \(2\pi\) would convert angular frequency back toward ordinary frequency, which is the reverse operation.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\omega=6\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\).

question:
Study the table and identify the row with the proper relation and unit.
RowQuantityRelationUnit
PFrequency\(f=\frac{1}{T}\)\(\text{Hz}\)
QAngular frequency\(\omega=\frac{T}{2\pi}\)\(\text{s}\)
RTime period\(T=f\)\(\text{Hz}\)
SAmplitude\(A=\omega T\)\(\text{rad s}^{-1}\)
explanation: Frequency and time period are reciprocal quantities, so \(f=\frac{1}{T}\). The SI unit of frequency is \(\text{Hz}\), equivalent to \(\text{s}^{-1}\). Angular frequency is \(\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi f\), not \(\frac{T}{2\pi}\). Time period is measured in \(\text{s}\), not in \(\text{Hz}\). Amplitude is a length measured in \(\text{m}\), so it cannot have the unit \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\).

question: A system completes \(15\) oscillations in \(30\,\text{s}\). Its angular frequency is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Number of oscillations \(N=15\), total time \(t=30\,\text{s}\).
First find the ordinary frequency:
\[
f=\frac{N}{t}
\]
Substitute the values:
\[
f=\frac{15}{30\,\text{s}}
\]
\[
f=0.5\,\text{s}^{-1}
\]
Now connect ordinary frequency with angular frequency:
\[
\omega=2\pi f
\]
Substitute \(f=0.5\,\text{s}^{-1}\):
\[
\omega=2\pi(0.5\,\text{s}^{-1})
\]
\[
\omega=\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
The calculation needs two stages: counting cycles per second first, then converting cycles to radians.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\omega=\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\).

question: Two oscillators have frequencies \(f_1=4\,\text{Hz}\) and \(f_2=8\,\text{Hz}\). The ratio of their time periods \(T_1:T_2\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(f_1=4\,\text{Hz}\) and \(f_2=8\,\text{Hz}\).
The relation between time period and frequency is
\[
T=\frac{1}{f}
\]
Therefore,
\[
T_1=\frac{1}{f_1}
\]
and
\[
T_2=\frac{1}{f_2}
\]
The ratio is
\[
\frac{T_1}{T_2}=\frac{\frac{1}{f_1}}{\frac{1}{f_2}}
\]
\[
\frac{T_1}{T_2}=\frac{f_2}{f_1}
\]
Substitute the frequencies:
\[
\frac{T_1}{T_2}=\frac{8}{4}=2
\]
So,
\[
T_1:T_2=2:1
\]
The oscillator with higher frequency has the smaller time period, so the ratio is the inverse of the frequency ratio.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(T_1:T_2=2:1\).

question: Two oscillators have time periods \(T_1=0.20\,\text{s}\) and \(T_2=0.40\,\text{s}\). The ratio of their angular frequencies \(\omega_1:\omega_2\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(T_1=0.20\,\text{s}\) and \(T_2=0.40\,\text{s}\).
Angular frequency is related to time period by
\[
\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}
\]
So angular frequency is inversely proportional to time period.
Write the ratio:
\[
\frac{\omega_1}{\omega_2}=\frac{\frac{2\pi}{T_1}}{\frac{2\pi}{T_2}}
\]
The factor \(2\pi\) cancels:
\[
\frac{\omega_1}{\omega_2}=\frac{T_2}{T_1}
\]
Substitute the values:
\[
\frac{\omega_1}{\omega_2}=\frac{0.40}{0.20}=2
\]
Thus,
\[
\omega_1:\omega_2=2:1
\]
The oscillator with the smaller time period has the larger angular frequency.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\omega_1:\omega_2=2:1\).

question: A learner writes that \(f\) and \(\omega\) are the same because both describe “how fast oscillation happens.” The best correction is that
opt_a: \(f\) counts cycles per second; \(\omega\) counts radians per second
opt_b: \(f\) is measured in \(\text{m}\), while \(\omega\) is measured in \(\text{s}\)
opt_c: \(f\) is always larger than \(\omega\) for every oscillator
opt_d: \(f\) applies only to pendulums, while \(\omega\) applies only to springs
explanation: Frequency \(f\) and angular frequency \(\omega\) both describe the rate of repetition, but they use different measures. Frequency \(f\) counts complete oscillations per second, so its unit is \(\text{Hz}\) or \(\text{s}^{-1}\). Angular frequency \(\omega\) gives the rate of phase change, so its unit is usually written as \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\). They are connected by \(\omega=2\pi f\), because one complete cycle corresponds to \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\). Treating them as identical misses the factor \(2\pi\) and can give wrong numerical values.

question:
Use the graph description below.
The displacement-time graph of an oscillator reaches positive maxima at \(t=0.10\,\text{s}\), \(t=0.50\,\text{s}\), and \(t=0.90\,\text{s}\). The shape of the graph repeats between successive positive maxima.
The angular frequency of the oscillator is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Reading the graph:} \) Successive positive maxima occur at \(0.10\,\text{s}\), \(0.50\,\text{s}\), and \(0.90\,\text{s}\).
The time gap between successive identical maxima is the time period \(T\).
\[
T=0.50\,\text{s}-0.10\,\text{s}
\]
\[
T=0.40\,\text{s}
\]
Angular frequency is
\[
\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}
\]
Substitute the period:
\[
\omega=\frac{2\pi}{0.40\,\text{s}}
\]
\[
\omega=5\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
The peak-to-peak time interval is used because the oscillator returns to the same displacement state at successive identical maxima.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\omega=5\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\).

question:
Study the table and choose the row with a unit mismatch.
RowQuantityUsual unit
PTime period \(T\)\(\text{s}\)
QFrequency \(f\)\(\text{Hz}\)
RAngular frequency \(\omega\)\(\text{rad s}^{-1}\)
SAmplitude \(A\)\(\text{Hz}\)
explanation: Time period \(T\) is a time, so its SI unit is \(\text{s}\). Frequency \(f\) counts cycles per second, so it is measured in \(\text{Hz}\). Angular frequency \(\omega\) measures phase change per second and is written in \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\). Amplitude \(A\) is maximum displacement from the mean position, so its unit must be a unit of length such as \(\text{m}\), not \(\text{Hz}\). The mismatch in row S comes from treating a size quantity as if it were a rate quantity.

question: If the angular frequency of an oscillator is doubled while its initial phase is unchanged, the immediate meaning is that
opt_a: the phase changes twice as fast with time
opt_b: the amplitude must become twice as large
opt_c: the displacement must remain positive forever
opt_d: the time period must also become twice as large
explanation: Angular frequency \(\omega\) measures how rapidly the phase of harmonic motion changes with time. In an expression such as \(\omega t+\phi\), increasing \(\omega\) makes the time-dependent part grow faster. This means the oscillator completes phase cycles more rapidly. Since \(T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}\), doubling \(\omega\) actually halves the time period, not doubles it. Amplitude is a separate quantity and does not automatically change just because \(\omega\) is changed.

question: Two oscillators complete \(20\) and \(30\) oscillations respectively in the same time interval. The ratio of their angular frequencies \(\omega_1:\omega_2\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Oscillator \(1\) completes \(20\) oscillations and oscillator \(2\) completes \(30\) oscillations in the same time interval.
Let the common time interval be \(t\).
Their frequencies are
\[
f_1=\frac{20}{t}
\]
and
\[
f_2=\frac{30}{t}
\]
So,
\[
f_1:f_2=20:30=2:3
\]
Angular frequency is related to frequency by
\[
\omega=2\pi f
\]
The same factor \(2\pi\) multiplies both frequencies, so the ratio of angular frequencies is the same as the ratio of ordinary frequencies.
\[
\omega_1:\omega_2=2:3
\]
The common time interval cancels because both oscillators are being compared over the same duration.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\omega_1:\omega_2=2:3\).

question: In the expression \(x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)\), the quantity \(\omega t+\phi\) is called the
explanation: In a harmonic expression, the argument of the sine or cosine function is called the phase. Here, the argument is \(\omega t+\phi\). The phase tells the stage of the oscillation at a given instant. The constant \(\phi\) is the initial phase, because it gives the phase at \(t=0\). Amplitude \(A\) controls the maximum displacement, while phase controls where the oscillator is within its cycle.

question: The initial phase \(\phi\) in \(x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)\) represents
opt_a: the phase of the oscillator at \(t=0\)
opt_b: the maximum speed of the oscillator
opt_c: the total distance covered in one oscillation
opt_d: the force constant of the oscillator
explanation: Initial phase \(\phi\) is the value of the phase when \(t=0\). Substituting \(t=0\) into \(\omega t+\phi\) gives \(\phi\). This constant decides the starting state of the oscillator in the chosen sine representation. It can change the initial displacement and direction of motion without changing the amplitude \(A\) or angular frequency \(\omega\). The initial phase is therefore a starting-condition quantity, not a measure of force or distance travelled.

question: Two oscillators have the same amplitude and frequency. At every instant, they have the same displacement and move in the same direction. Their phase difference is
explanation: If two oscillators always have the same displacement and move in the same direction, they are in the same stage of oscillation at every instant. This condition is called being in phase. For in-phase oscillations, the phase difference is \(0\) or any integral multiple of \(2\pi\). Among the given options, \(0\) represents this relation most directly. A phase difference of \(\pi\) would make them opposite in displacement at the same instant.

question: Two identical oscillators have equal amplitudes and equal frequencies, but whenever one is at \(+A\), the other is at \(-A\). Their phase difference is most simply
explanation: If one oscillator is at \(+A\) while the other is at \(-A\), they are at opposite extremes at the same instant. For equal-amplitude harmonic oscillations of the same frequency, this corresponds to a phase difference of \(\pi\). Such oscillators are often described as being in opposite phase. A phase difference of \(0\) would place them in the same state. A phase difference of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) would place one oscillator a quarter cycle ahead of the other, not at the opposite extreme in this situation.

question: A body in harmonic motion is observed at the same displacement \(x\) two times during one cycle. The two observations need not represent the same state because
opt_a: the direction of motion may be different
opt_b: the amplitude must be different at the two instants
opt_c: the time period becomes zero at one of the instants
opt_d: the phase is never connected with displacement
explanation: In harmonic motion, the same displacement can be reached while the body is moving in opposite directions. For example, a body may pass a point while moving toward the positive extreme and later pass the same point while returning toward the mean position. The displacement value alone does not fully specify the state of motion. Phase contains more information because it tells the stage of the cycle, including the direction when combined with the harmonic function. This is why two equal displacement readings can correspond to different velocities.

question:
Consider the following statements about phase in harmonic motion.
I. Phase tells the stage of oscillation.
II. Initial phase depends on the chosen starting instant and representation.
III. Same displacement always means same direction of motion.
Select the valid set.
explanation: Phase tells where the oscillator is in its cycle, so statement I is valid. Initial phase depends on the condition of the oscillator at the chosen \(t=0\) and also on whether sine or cosine form is used, so statement II is valid. Statement III is not valid because the same displacement can occur once while the body moves in one direction and again while it moves in the opposite direction. Displacement is only one part of the motion state. The phase description helps remove this ambiguity.

question:
Read the situation below and answer the question.
Two identical oscillators start from the mean position at the same instant. Oscillator P starts moving toward the positive side, while oscillator Q starts moving toward the negative side. Both have the same amplitude and frequency.
The simplest phase difference between P and Q is
explanation: Both oscillators start from the mean position, so their initial displacement is the same. However, they start moving in opposite directions. For harmonic oscillators with the same amplitude and frequency, opposite directions at the same mean position correspond to opposite phases. A phase difference of \(\pi\) makes one oscillator the negative of the other at corresponding instants. A phase difference of \(0\) would require the same displacement and the same direction of motion at the same time.

question: The phase of a harmonic oscillator changes by \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\) in
explanation: A complete harmonic cycle corresponds to a full phase change of \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\). After this phase change, the oscillator returns to the same displacement and the same direction of motion. A phase change of \(\pi\,\text{rad}\) corresponds to half a cycle, where the displacement is opposite for equal amplitude motion. A phase change of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\,\text{rad}\) corresponds to a quarter cycle. The phrase “same state” requires both position and direction to repeat, which occurs after \(2\pi\,\text{rad}\).

question: If two harmonic oscillations of the same frequency differ in phase by \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), the time difference between corresponding states is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Phase difference \(\Delta\phi=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
In one complete period \(T\), phase changes by \(2\pi\).
So the fraction of the period corresponding to phase difference \(\Delta\phi\) is
\[
\frac{\Delta t}{T}=\frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi}
\]
Substitute \(\Delta\phi=\frac{\pi}{2}\):
\[
\frac{\Delta t}{T}=\frac{\frac{\pi}{2}}{2\pi}
\]
\[
\frac{\Delta t}{T}=\frac{1}{4}
\]
Therefore,
\[
\Delta t=\frac{T}{4}
\]
A phase difference of \(\pi\) would correspond to \(\frac{T}{2}\), not \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\Delta t=\frac{T}{4}\).

question: A harmonic oscillator has phase \(\omega t+\phi\). When \(t=0\), its phase is \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). The value of \(\phi\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Phase is \(\omega t+\phi\).
At \(t=0\), the phase becomes
\[
\omega(0)+\phi
\]
\[
=\phi
\]
The given phase at \(t=0\) is \(\frac{\pi}{3}\).
Therefore,
\[
\phi=\frac{\pi}{3}
\]
This shows why \(\phi\) is called the initial phase.
It records the starting phase value of the oscillator in the chosen mathematical form.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\phi=\frac{\pi}{3}\).

question: A harmonic motion is described by the phase \(\theta=4\pi t+\frac{\pi}{2}\), where \(t\) is in \(\text{s}\). The angular frequency is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given phase form:} \)
\[
\theta=4\pi t+\frac{\pi}{2}
\]
The standard phase form is
\[
\theta=\omega t+\phi
\]
Compare the coefficient of \(t\) in both expressions.
In the given expression, the coefficient of \(t\) is \(4\pi\).
Therefore,
\[
\omega=4\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
The constant term \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) is the initial phase, not the angular frequency.
The angular frequency is identified from the term multiplying time.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\omega=4\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\).

question:
A table compares phase descriptions for harmonic oscillators of the same frequency.
RowPhase relationPhysical meaning
PPhase difference \(0\)Same stage of oscillation
QPhase difference \(\pi\)Opposite phase
RPhase difference \(\frac{\pi}{2}\)Quarter-cycle separation
SPhase difference \(2\pi\)Never returns to the same state
The row that needs correction is
explanation: A phase difference of \(0\) means two oscillations are in the same stage, so row P is suitable. A phase difference of \(\pi\) means opposite phase for equal-frequency harmonic oscillations, so row Q is suitable. A phase difference of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) corresponds to a quarter-cycle separation, so row R is also suitable. A phase change of \(2\pi\) brings an oscillator back to the same state, not to a state that never returns. Row S reverses the meaning of a full phase cycle.

question: A harmonic displacement is written as \(x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)\). In this expression, the quantity \(A\) fixes
opt_a: the maximum displacement from the mean position
opt_b: the number of radians in one complete cycle
opt_c: the direction of acceleration at all positions
opt_d: the time measured from the start of motion
explanation: In \(x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)\), the sine factor varies between \(-1\) and \(+1\). Therefore, the largest possible value of \(x\) is \(+A\), and the smallest possible value is \(-A\). This makes \(A\) the amplitude, or maximum magnitude of displacement from the mean position. The phase \(\omega t+\phi\) decides the stage of the oscillation, while \(\omega\) controls how fast the phase changes. The amplitude controls the size of the motion, not the rate at which the cycle is completed.

question: The equations \(x=A\sin\omega t\) and \(x=A\cos\omega t\) can describe the same type of harmonic motion because
opt_a: sine represents displacement while cosine represents force only
opt_b: sine has no amplitude but cosine has amplitude
opt_c: cosine is periodic but sine is never periodic
opt_d: sine and cosine differ only by a phase shift
explanation: Sine and cosine are both periodic functions with the same shape and period. A cosine function can be written as a sine function with a phase shift, since \(\cos\theta=\sin(\theta+\frac{\pi}{2})\). Therefore, choosing sine or cosine mainly changes the phase constant needed to describe the initial state. The physical motion can still have the same amplitude \(A\) and angular frequency \(\omega\). The choice of sine or cosine is a matter of starting condition, not a change in the kind of harmonic motion.

question: For the displacement equation \(x=0.08\cos(10\pi t)\), where \(x\) is in \(\text{m}\) and \(t\) is in \(\text{s}\), the amplitude and time period are respectively
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given equation:} \)
\[
x=0.08\cos(10\pi t)
\]
Compare it with the standard form:
\[
x=A\cos(\omega t+\phi)
\]
The coefficient outside the cosine function gives the amplitude:
\[
A=0.08\,\text{m}
\]
The coefficient of \(t\) inside the cosine argument gives angular frequency:
\[
\omega=10\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
Use the relation:
\[
T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}
\]
Substitute \(\omega=10\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\):
\[
T=\frac{2\pi}{10\pi}\,\text{s}
\]
\[
T=0.20\,\text{s}
\]
The value \(10\pi\) is not the amplitude because it multiplies time inside the phase.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(A=0.08\,\text{m}\) and \(T=0.20\,\text{s}\).

question: A displacement equation is \(x=5\sin(2\pi t+\frac{\pi}{6})\), where \(x\) is in \(\text{cm}\) and \(t\) is in \(\text{s}\). At \(t=0\), the displacement is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given equation:} \)
\[
x=5\sin(2\pi t+\frac{\pi}{6})
\]
At \(t=0\), substitute \(t=0\):
\[
x=5\sin(2\pi(0)+\frac{\pi}{6})
\]
\[
x=5\sin\frac{\pi}{6}
\]
Use the standard value:
\[
\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{1}{2}
\]
So,
\[
x=5\times\frac{1}{2}\,\text{cm}
\]
\[
x=2.5\,\text{cm}
\]
The amplitude is \(5\,\text{cm}\), but the initial displacement is not equal to amplitude unless the phase makes the sine value \(+1\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(x=2.5\,\text{cm}\).

question:
Study the table and identify the row that correctly reads the equation \(x=0.04\sin(8t+\frac{\pi}{3})\), where \(x\) is in \(\text{m}\) and \(t\) is in \(\text{s}\).
RowAmplitudeAngular frequencyInitial phase
P\(0.04\,\text{m}\)\(8\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\)\(\frac{\pi}{3}\)

explanation: The standard sine form is \(x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)\). In \(x=0.04\sin(8t+\frac{\pi}{3})\), the coefficient outside the sine function is the amplitude, so \(A=0.04\,\text{m}\). The coefficient of \(t\) inside the phase is the angular frequency, so \(\omega=8\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\). The constant term inside the phase is the initial phase, so \(\phi=\frac{\pi}{3}\). Row P keeps the outside coefficient, the time coefficient, and the constant phase term in their proper roles.

question: A harmonic oscillator is described by \(x=A\cos\omega t\). Its displacement at \(t=0\) is
explanation: For the equation \(x=A\cos\omega t\), put \(t=0\). The phase then becomes \(\omega(0)=0\). Since \(\cos0=1\), the displacement is \(x=A(1)=A\). This means the oscillator starts from the positive extreme in this particular representation. In contrast, \(x=A\sin\omega t\) would give \(x=0\) at \(t=0\), showing how sine and cosine forms represent different starting conditions.

question: A harmonic oscillator is described by \(x=A\sin\omega t\). The first time after \(t=0\) when it reaches \(x=A\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given equation:} \)
\[
x=A\sin\omega t
\]
The oscillator reaches \(x=A\) when
\[
\sin\omega t=1
\]
The first positive phase for which this happens is
\[
\omega t=\frac{\pi}{2}
\]
Thus,
\[
t=\frac{\pi}{2\omega}
\]
Since
\[
T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}
\]
we can write
\[
\frac{T}{4}=\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{2\pi}{\omega}
\]
\[
\frac{T}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2\omega}
\]
So the first positive extreme is reached after one-quarter of a period.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(t=\frac{T}{4}\).

question:
Read the situation below and answer the question.
Two equations are proposed for the same oscillator: \(x=A\sin\omega t\) and \(x=A\sin(\omega t+\pi)\). The amplitude and angular frequency are the same in both equations.
How are the displacements in the two equations related at the same instant?
opt_b: The first has twice the amplitude of the second
opt_d: They are always opposite in sign
explanation: The two equations have the same \(A\) and \(\omega\), so they describe oscillations of the same size and rate. The difference is the extra phase \(\pi\) in the second equation. Since \(\sin(\theta+\pi)=-\sin\theta\), the second displacement is the negative of the first at the same instant. This means the oscillators are in opposite phase. The amplitude is not changed by adding \(\pi\) to the phase; only the stage of the cycle is shifted.

question: A displacement-time graph is described by a sine curve whose peak value is \(6\,\text{cm}\) and whose time between two successive positive peaks is \(0.50\,\text{s}\). The equation can have the form
explanation:
\( \textbf{Graph information:} \) Peak value \(=6\,\text{cm}\), so \(A=6\,\text{cm}\).
The time between successive positive peaks is the time period:
\[
T=0.50\,\text{s}
\]
Angular frequency is
\[
\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}
\]
Substitute \(T=0.50\,\text{s}\):
\[
\omega=\frac{2\pi}{0.50}
\]
\[
\omega=4\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
So a suitable sine form is
\[
x=6\sin(4\pi t+\phi)\,\text{cm}
\]
The coefficient outside the sine gives amplitude, while the coefficient of \(t\) inside the phase gives angular frequency.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(x=6\sin(4\pi t+\phi)\,\text{cm}\).

question: The defining acceleration condition for simple harmonic motion is that acceleration is
opt_a: constant in magnitude and always along the motion
opt_b: proportional to displacement and directed away from the mean position
opt_c: proportional to displacement and directed toward the mean position
opt_d: zero at every point of the motion
explanation: Simple harmonic motion requires a special kind of restoring acceleration. Its magnitude is proportional to the magnitude of displacement from the mean position. Its direction is always toward the mean position, opposite to the displacement vector in one-dimensional notation. This condition is written as \(a=-\omega^2x\). The negative sign is essential because it shows that acceleration and displacement have opposite signs for a chosen positive axis.

question: Among the following acceleration-displacement relations, the one that represents simple harmonic motion is
explanation: In simple harmonic motion, acceleration must be directly proportional to displacement and opposite in direction. The general form is \(a=-\omega^2x\), where \(\omega^2\) is a positive constant. The relation \(a=-4x\) matches this form with \(\omega^2=4\,\text{s}^{-2}\). The relation \(a=+4x\) has acceleration in the same direction as displacement, so it does not describe a restoring acceleration. The relation \(a=-4x^2\) is not linear in \(x\), so it does not satisfy the basic SHM condition.

question:
Assertion: In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration is zero at the mean position.
Reason: In simple harmonic motion, \(a=-\omega^2x\), and the displacement \(x\) is zero at the mean position.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: In SHM, acceleration is given by \(a=-\omega^2x\). At the mean position, the displacement from the mean position is \(x=0\). Substituting \(x=0\) gives \(a=0\). The Reason states both the mathematical relation and the position condition needed to explain the Assertion. This does not mean the body is necessarily at rest at the mean position; it only means the restoring acceleration is zero there.

question:
Study the table and identify the row that correctly gives acceleration direction in one-dimensional SHM when the positive direction is to the right.

explanation: In one-dimensional SHM, \(a=-\omega^2x\). If the body is to the right of the mean position, \(x\) is positive. The negative sign in \(a=-\omega^2x\) then makes acceleration negative, which means toward the left. This is the restoring direction, back toward the mean position. If the body is left of the mean position, acceleration would be toward the right, so row R has the wrong direction.

question: A body in SHM has \(\omega=5\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\). When its displacement is \(x=0.020\,\text{m}\), its acceleration is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(\omega=5\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\), \(x=0.020\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required:} \) Acceleration \(a\).
For SHM, the acceleration-displacement relation is
\[
a=-\omega^2x
\]
This relation applies because acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed toward the mean position.
Substitute the values:
\[
a=-(5)^2(0.020)
\]
\[
a=-(25)(0.020)
\]
\[
a=-0.50\,\text{m s}^{-2}
\]
The negative sign means the acceleration is opposite to the positive displacement.
The magnitude is \(0.50\,\text{m s}^{-2}\), but the signed acceleration is negative for \(x\gt0\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(a=-0.50\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).

question: A graph is plotted between acceleration \(a\) and displacement \(x\) for a body in SHM. The graph is a straight line through the origin with negative slope. The slope represents
explanation:
For SHM, acceleration and displacement are related by
\[
a=-\omega^2x
\]
This has the graph form
\[
y=mx
\]
if \(a\) is plotted on the vertical axis and \(x\) on the horizontal axis.
The slope is the coefficient of \(x\):
\[
\text{slope}=-\omega^2
\]
The negative sign shows that acceleration is opposite in direction to displacement.
The graph passes through the origin because \(a=0\) when \(x=0\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The slope is \(-\omega^2\).

question: A motion has acceleration \(a=-9x\), where \(x\) is measured from the mean position in \(\text{m}\) and \(a\) is in \(\text{m s}^{-2}\). The angular frequency of the motion is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given relation:} \)
\[
a=-9x
\]
The standard SHM acceleration relation is
\[
a=-\omega^2x
\]
Compare the coefficient of \(x\) in both equations:
\[
\omega^2=9
\]
Take the positive square root for angular frequency:
\[
\omega=3\,\text{rad s}^{-1}
\]
The value \(9\) is \(\omega^2\), not \(\omega\).
Angular frequency is reported in \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\), while \(\omega^2\) has the dimension of \(\text{s}^{-2}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\omega=3\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\).

question: A body has acceleration \(a=-16x\), where \(x\) is displacement from the mean position. The motion is simple harmonic because
opt_a: acceleration is constant at all positions
opt_b: acceleration is always in the positive direction
opt_d: acceleration is linear in \(x\) and restoring
explanation: The defining condition for SHM is \(a=-\omega^2x\). In the given relation \(a=-16x\), acceleration is proportional to displacement \(x\). The negative sign shows that acceleration is directed opposite to displacement, so it is toward the mean position. This is exactly the restoring acceleration condition required for simple harmonic motion. A constant acceleration would not give the usual SHM condition, because the acceleration must change with displacement from the mean position.

question: A one-dimensional motion is described by \(a=-25x\). The time period of the motion is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given relation:} \)

The standard acceleration relation for SHM is

a=-\omega^2x

Compare the two relations:
\[

\]
The time period is related to angular frequency by
\[
T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}
\]
Substitute \(\omega=5\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\):
\[
T=\frac{2\pi}{5}\,\text{s}
\]
The coefficient \(25\) gives \(\omega^2\), not \(\omega\), so using \(25\) directly as angular frequency would give the wrong period.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(T=\frac{2\pi}{5}\,\text{s}\).

question: A displacement \(x\) is measured from the mean position. Which force-displacement relation can produce simple harmonic motion of a particle of mass \(m\)?
explanation: For a particle to perform SHM, the net force must be proportional to displacement and directed toward the mean position. The relation \(F=-kx\) satisfies this condition when \(k\) is a positive constant. If \(x\) is positive, the force is negative, and if \(x\) is negative, the force is positive. The relation \(F=+kx\) pushes the particle away from the mean position, so it does not provide a restoring force. A force proportional to \(x^2\) is not linear in displacement, so it does not match the simple harmonic condition.

question:
Study the table and identify the row that does not satisfy the SHM condition when \(x\) is measured from the mean position.
